concepts.name: Reserve Bank of India: Ownership, Structure, and Dual Role
key_dimensions: Nationalization in 1949 vs. establishment in 1935 under RBI Act — common confusion point
Banker to Banks vs. Banker to Government — dual role distinctions and limits
RBI's role as 'Lender of Last Resort' — conditions and instruments used (LAF, MSF)
Autonomy vs. Government control debate — Section 7 of RBI Act and its invocation

concepts.name: Scheduled vs. Non-Scheduled Banks: Classification Criteria
key_dimensions: Inclusion in Second Schedule of RBI Act 1934 — eligibility conditions (paid-up capital ≥ ₹5 lakh, satisfaction of RBI)
Privileges of scheduled banks — access to RBI credit, clearing house membership
Non-scheduled banks — still regulated by RBI but not entitled to scheduled bank benefits
UPSC trap: All nationalized banks are scheduled, but not all scheduled banks are nationalized

concepts.name: Nationalized Banks: History, Rationale, and Current Status
key_dimensions: Two phases: 14 banks in 1969 (>₹50 crore deposits) and 6 banks in 1980 (>₹200 crore deposits)
Legal basis: Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and 1980
Merger wave post-2017: reduction from 27 to 12 public sector banks — which banks merged with which
UPSC trap: SBI and its associates are NOT covered under 1970/1980 Acts — separate SBI Act 1955

concepts.name: State Bank of India: Special Constitutional and Legal Status
key_dimensions: Established under SBI Act 1955 — distinct from nationalization acts of 1969/1980
Government shareholding through RBI until 2007 — transfer to GoI via SBI (Amendment) Act 2007
Merger of associate banks (2017) and Bharatiya Mahila Bank — exam-relevant sequence
SBI as an agent of RBI in states where RBI has no office — agency banking arrangement

concepts.name: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs): Ownership, Mandate, and Reforms
key_dimensions: Established under RRB Act 1976 — Narasimham Committee recommendation
Tripartite ownership: Central Govt 50%, Sponsor Bank 35%, State Govt 15% — exact ratios frequently tested
Mandate: credit to small farmers, artisans, agricultural laborers in rural areas
Consolidation: from 196 RRBs (2005) to ~43 RRBs (2023) — One State-One RRB policy
UPSC trap: RRBs are scheduled commercial banks but NOT nationalized banks

concepts.name: Cooperative Banks: Structure, Regulation, and the Dual Control Problem
key_dimensions: Three-tier structure: State Cooperative Banks → District Central Cooperative Banks → Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)
Dual regulation: RBI for banking functions + Registrar of Cooperative Societies (state) for management — classic overlap
Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act 2020 — extended RBI's supervisory powers to Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs)
UPSC trap: PACS are NOT regulated by RBI; they fall solely under state cooperative laws
Urban Cooperative Banks vs. Rural Cooperative Banks — different regulatory treatment

concepts.name: Small Finance Banks (SFBs): Licensing, Objectives, and Restrictions
key_dimensions: RBI guidelines 2015 — differentiated banking license concept
Mandatory: 75% of ANBC to priority sector; 50% of loan portfolio in tickets ≤ ₹25 lakh
Eligible promoters: NBFCs, MFIs, LABs, cooperative banks — not new entrants without track record
UPSC trap: SFBs CAN offer all basic banking services unlike Payment Banks — key distinction
Conversion pathway: SFBs can apply for universal bank license after 5 years (SFB 'on tap' guidelines)

concepts.name: Payments Banks: Scope, Restrictions, and Business Model
key_dimensions: RBI guidelines 2014 (Nachiket Mor Committee) — cannot issue credit cards or give loans
Maximum deposit limit per customer: ₹2 lakh (revised from ₹1 lakh in 2021)
Must invest minimum 75% of demand deposits in SLR-eligible government securities
UPSC trap: Payments Banks CANNOT lend — this is their defining restriction vs. SFBs
Current active players vs. those who surrendered licenses — India Post Payments Bank special status

concepts.name: Local Area Banks (LABs): Features, Failure, and Legacy
key_dimensions: Established 1996 — private, geographically restricted to 2-3 contiguous districts
Objective: mobilize rural savings and channel credit in specific regions
Only 2 LABs operational currently (out of 5 licensed) — Coastal Local Area Bank, Krishna Bhima Samruddhi
UPSC trap: LABs predate SFBs — SFBs essentially replaced the LAB concept at a larger scale
Comparison with RRBs: both are rural-focused but differ in ownership and area of operation

concepts.name: NABARD: Classification, Functions, and Refinancing Role
key_dimensions: Established 1982 under NABARD Act — based on B. Sivaraman Committee recommendations
NOT a commercial bank — it is an apex development finance institution (DFI)
Refinancing role for RRBs, cooperative banks, and state land development banks
UPSC trap: NABARD regulates RRBs (inspection/supervision) but RBI regulates cooperative banks — division of oversight
NABARD's role in Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) marketplace

concepts.name: SIDBI, NHB, and EXIM Bank: Sectoral Development Banks
key_dimensions: SIDBI (1990): refinancing for MSMEs — subsidiary of IDBI initially, now independent
NHB (1988): regulates Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) — recently supervision transferred to RBI (2019)
EXIM Bank (1982): financing exports and imports — functions under Ministry of Finance
UPSC trap: NHB regulation of HFCs transferred to RBI — post-IL&FS crisis regulatory change
These are NOT scheduled commercial banks — they are apex refinancing/development institutions

concepts.name: Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs): Classification and Regulatory Arbitrage
key_dimensions: Cannot accept demand deposits — key distinction from banks
Not part of payment and settlement system — cannot issue cheques
Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework 2021: Base, Middle, Upper, Top Layer — replacing old categories
UPSC trap: NBFCs are regulated by RBI under Chapter III-B of RBI Act, NOT Banking Regulation Act
Systematically Important NBFCs (SI-NBFCs): asset size ≥ ₹500 crore — stricter norms

concepts.name: Microfinance Institutions (MFIs) and NBFC-MFIs: Regulatory Framework
key_dimensions: NBFC-MFI: specific category of NBFC regulated by RBI — must have ≥75% qualifying assets as microfinance loans
RBI Microfinance Guidelines 2022: income ceiling for borrower households (rural ₹1.25 lakh, urban ₹2 lakh)
Malegam Committee recommendations — foundation of NBFC-MFI regulation
UPSC trap: Not all MFIs are NBFC-MFIs — Section 8 companies (NGO-MFIs) and cooperative MFIs have different regulators
Collateral-free lending and household income-based repayment capacity assessment — key features

concepts.name: Priority Sector Lending (PSL): Targets, Categories, and Bank-wise Variations
key_dimensions: Overall PSL target: 40% of ANBC for domestic commercial banks and foreign banks (>20 branches)
Sub-targets: Agriculture 18% (of which 10% to small/marginal farmers), Weaker Sections 12%
UPSC trap: Foreign banks with <20 branches have different PSL targets (40% but different sub-categories)
RRBs and SFBs have 75% PSL target — much higher than commercial banks
PSL Certificates (PSLCs): tradeable certificates to meet shortfall — four types (General, SF/MF, Agriculture, Micro)

concepts.name: Differential Banking Licenses: Concept and Regulatory Philosophy
key_dimensions: Nachiket Mor Committee 2014 — recommended differentiated/tiered banking structure
Principle: specialized banks for niche segments rather than one-size-fits-all universal banking
Four types of differentiated licenses: Payments Banks, SFBs, Wholesale and Long-Term Finance (WLTF) Banks (proposed, never implemented), Custodian Banks
UPSC trap: WLTF Banks were recommended but never actually licensed — distinguish recommended vs. implemented
'On Tap' licensing for universal banks and SFBs — continuous application window since 2016/2019

concepts.name: Banking Regulation Act 1949: Scope, Applicability, and Key Provisions
key_dimensions: Does NOT apply to primary agricultural credit societies and cooperative land mortgage banks — UPSC trap
Applies to cooperative banks (after 2020 amendment) for UCBs — recent change
Key powers given to RBI: licensing, branch expansion, inspection, supersession of board, merger/amalgamation
Section 35A: RBI's power to give directions — basis of most RBI regulatory actions
UPSC trap: SBI is governed by SBI Act 1955, NOT primarily by Banking Regulation Act

concepts.name: Basel Norms and Capital Adequacy: Application Across Bank Types
key_dimensions: Basel III implementation in India — Capital Conservation Buffer, Countercyclical Buffer, Leverage Ratio
Minimum Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR): 9% in India vs. 8% under Basel III — India's stricter norm
Differential application: Payments Banks and SFBs have separate capital requirements
UPSC trap: Cooperative banks and RRBs have different CRAR requirements than commercial banks
Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework — triggered by CRAR breach, NPA levels, Return on Assets

concepts.name: Deposit Insurance: DICGC Coverage and Bank-wise Applicability
key_dimensions: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) — subsidiary of RBI
Current coverage: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank (revised from ₹1 lakh in 2020)
UPSC trap: Covers commercial banks, RRBs, cooperative banks — does NOT cover Primary Cooperative Societies
DICGC Amendment Act 2021: time-bound repayment within 90 days even during bank moratorium — significant reform
Does NOT cover government deposits, inter-bank deposits — exclusions frequently tested

concepts.name: Lead Bank Scheme and Financial Inclusion Architecture
key_dimensions: Lead Bank Scheme 1969 (S. Narasimham Committee) — one bank assigned lead role per district
District Credit Plan (DCP) and Annual Credit Plan (ACP) — tools under Lead Bank Scheme
UPSC trap: Lead Bank is NOT the only bank operating in a district — it is a coordinating role
Business Correspondent (BC) Model — RBI permitted non-bank entities as BCs for last-mile delivery
Relationship with PMJDY: Lead banks responsible for coverage targets under financial inclusion plans

concepts.name: India Post Payments Bank (IPPB): Unique Features and Strategic Importance
key_dimensions: Set up as a public sector company under Department of Posts — 100% GoI ownership
Largest financial inclusion network — leverages 1.5 lakh post offices and ~3 lakh postmen/gramin dak sevaks
UPSC trap: IPPB is a Payments Bank — cannot lend, maximum ₹2 lakh deposit per customer
Interoperability with postal savings schemes — but IPPB accounts and post office savings accounts are separate
Strategic significance: reaching unbanked rural population beyond commercial bank BC network
